blindSummary:
This country's risk picture is anchored by one of the world's most institutionalised indigenous third-gender traditions. The country's two indigenous third-gender identities are culturally embedded: recognised as heirs to customary land and eligible for customary chiefly titles within the indigenous social system, organised nationally through a formal association (a recognised stakeholder in the UN human-rights review process since 1987), and visible through a well-known community pageant culture. This country repealed its colonial-era "female impersonation" crime in 2013, so no law touches gender expression itself.

The remaining negatives are modest for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition (both resident-facing); documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against third-gender people (a peer-led study by a regional trans-network — primarily resident/domestic contexts); isolated police-harassment reports (2 respondents, no convictions); and village councils that enforce conservative dress and behaviour norms. The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for a fraction of visitors, not a trans-universal one.
blindOutOfScope: Cultural embedding of the indigenous third-gender role is an informal protection; criminalisation unenforced.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional trans-network convening report (May 2024): recap of a convening hosted in a neighbouring island country - brought together gender-diverse community members from across the island region (including this country and several neighbours and territories) on health and well-being, intersectionality and legal gender recognition.

NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying international legal-aid trust country profile documents this country's criminalisation of same-sex activity (up to 5 years under a 2013 crimes statute).

National third-gender association's stakeholder report for this country's UN review (39th session, 2021): on protecting the rights of third-gender and LGBTIQ people - describes the culturally unique indigenous third-gender identities and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news-agency feature covers this country's third-gender community delicately balancing sex and religion.
NOTE: the regional trans-network's country socio-economic study returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

Foreign public broadcaster's regional service (May 2013): relief in the indigenous third-gender community at removal of the impersonation crime - under the new criminal code the crime of 'impersonating a woman' was scrapped; the national association's president describes the relief (the section had not been enforced for decades but could have been revived); notes the sodomy provision remains and the community is not agitating about it.

Academic journal monograph on the country's third-gender role (Aug 2001): analysis of the indigenous identity (a term glossed as 'in the manner of a woman') - biological males expressing feminine gender identities; argues the role is both viewed through and reshaped by imported discourses of sexuality; notes that the region's largest city, in a neighbouring country, hosts considerable populations of this and a related island third-gender identity.

UN equality campaign information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status across the island region - documents this country's indigenous third-gender role (shared with two nearby territories of the same culture) among the diverse pre-colonial island gender identities described as important parts of the region's cultural heritage.
blindLocalsOnly: The discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against third-gender people - documented in a peer-led study by a regional trans-network - occur primarily in resident/domestic contexts; village-council norms govern resident life.
blindTangential: The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for visitors travelling with partners, not a trans-universal one.
